claims.text: High configurational entropy governs the structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a single-phase solid solution over intermetallic formation or phase segregation.
High configurational entropy minimizes atomic diffusion in HEA nanoparticles.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, near-equiatomic, single-phase HEAs with a uniform lattice structure.
Selectively depleting one constituent from an initially near-equiatomic nanoparticle lowers its configurational entropy.
An inert or controlled service atmosphere minimizes extrinsic oxidative effects.
High configurational entropy enforces a disordered but stable atomic distribution in the nanoparticle.
High configurational entropy produces a uniform coordination environment across an HEA nanoparticle.
Configurational entropy lowers the free-energy difference between the single solid solution and segregated phases.
The entropy-induced free-energy change suppresses phase segregation and intermetallic precipitation under thermal stress.
Low atomic diffusion maintains uniform active sites needed for catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
Pristine high-entropy nanoparticles will exhibit less phase separation and lower atomic diffusion than element-depleted nanoparticles.
Pristine high-entropy nanoparticles will retain catalytic performance better than entropy-reduced nanoparticles.
Pristine high-entropy nanoparticles will retain thermoelectric performance better than entropy-reduced nanoparticles.
The proposed entropy-stability relationship applies throughout 773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric operation.
HEA nanoparticles can catalyze HER, ORR, and OER, making these reactions relevant catalytic test cases.
Statistically indistinguishable structural and performance stability between pristine and entropy-reduced particles would falsify the assertion that high configurational entropy governs stability.

contradictions.description: The falsification rule invokes catalytic and thermoelectric stability, but the listed performance measurements are electrochemical catalytic tests only; no thermoelectric property or stability measurement is specified.

The hypothesis attributes low atomic diffusivity to configurational entropy, whereas the cited HEA evidence attributes low diffusivity to severe lattice distortion caused by constituent atomic-size differences.
